newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD striving for May investment freedom treaty.
newsitem.headline: OECD striving for May investment freedom treaty.

text.p: The OECD is working at full speed to prepare a draft treaty on the removal of investment restrictions for its annual ministers' meeting in May, deputy secretary general Joanna Shelton said on Friday.

Shelton, speaking at a press lunch at the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development's headquarters, said she hoped the treaty would be legally binding and that it would be open to signing by non-members of the 29-country organisation.
"We're now in the closing five months of what we hope will be an agreement extending legal protection to investors," she said. "We're optimistic but nothing's agreed. We hope to conclude by May."
"We're trying to bind these into a treaty which would be legally binding," Shelton said, adding that working groups would dedicate one week a month until May to try to get a text ready for ministers.
The idea is to commit signatories to treat domestic and foreign investors alike and remove obstacles to international investment, she said.
"I hope it will cover portfolio investment and intangible investment such as intellectual property," said Shelton, an American who worked on trade issues in the United States.

There were already signs that some non-member countries could be attracted to sign up, she said. Other OECD officials made it clear, however, that non-OECD countries were unlikely to take any formal position until they saw the final pact.

The treaty is, at this stage, the big item for the ministerial-level meeting in May. The OECD meeting usually gathers a range of medium-ranking trade, industry and finance ministers from member countries.

Shelton said some the toughest issues still to be worked out included how to lift restrictions on investment by foreigners when companies were being privatised as well as restrictions on investment in specific economic sectors.

She also said another tough issue to tackle was concern in some countries that agreement could be reached at national level, only to be undone at a lower level in countries with a federal structure such as Germany or the United States.
